initial_requirements: Public health organizations need an outbreak management system to support investigation, monitoring, analysis, and reporting during disease outbreaks, bioterrorism incidents, and other health events. Investigators should be able to collect information about cases, contacts, exposures, specimens, and interventions, connect related entities and events, and use the resulting information to identify and contain a health threat while protecting sensitive data.

slots.key: Offline access and sync for field work
slots.value: Investigators should be able to access only the cases and data they already have permission to see when offline, with sensitive fields tightly restricted. They can draft notes and queue certain updates while offline, but anything that could overwrite someone else’s work must wait for sync and conflict checking when they reconnect. If the case changed while they were away, the system should preserve both the offline submission and the newer online version for reviewer reconciliation instead of silently replacing one with the other. During downtime or recovery, staff also need a way to capture new cases, contacts, exposures, and critical actions through temporary offline logging or paper/emergency forms, then cleanly hand those entries back into the system later without losing timestamps, ownership, or links between records; read-only access to existing case details would also be helpful during recovery. For field work entered later, the business record should keep the original action time and not automatically re-date it to the entry time. If someone needs to use the entry time for a specific reason, that should be explicit and visible, but the default business record should stay anchored to when the action actually happened.

slots.key: Batch import creation and update rules
slots.value: Batch imports can create new investigations when the match is clear; updates from other systems should flag differences and require authorized staff to decide which version to keep when there is any uncertainty. slots.key: Operating environment and long-running follow-up assumptions

slots.key: Edit separation and restriction rules for linked records
slots.value: The shared case should hold the core investigation status and overall summary, while linked people, contacts, exposures, and actions should be editable separately if they belong to different parts of the investigation. Investigators should only edit what their role and assignment allow, and some linked details like identifying information, lab results, or sensitive interview notes may need to stay restricted to a smaller group for legal or public health reasons. If a linked record is being used in multiple active workflows, the system should control edits carefully so one team cannot accidentally overwrite information another team still depends on. The person who has the record actively assigned or checked out for an urgent task gets edit priority first; everyone else sees it read-only or works on a draft. If the record is important enough that conflicting changes would be risky, the system should lock it briefly or require supervisor approval before the change is committed. If two updates still collide, the system should keep both, flag the conflict immediately, and have a reviewer decide which version becomes the operative one. A shared record should be locked or require supervisor approval when the change affects case status, exposure classification, contact tracing assignments, or anything that could change who is notified or what public health action happens next. Approval is also expected when the record is already being edited by someone else, or when the user is trying to change restricted sensitive data. A time-critical containment update, such as a positive lab result or urgent isolation action, may bypass the restriction if a qualified supervisor or designated responder forces the update, but the system must log exactly why and alert the other users. Access should be based on role, jurisdiction, and need to know, with the default being as narrow as possible for anything sensitive or restricted. If a record is tied to a specific investigation, only the assigned team and the people supporting that jurisdiction should be able to view or edit it, and notes with especially sensitive details should be even more limited. Access can be broadened only when it’s necessary for coordinated response or supervision, but things like protected informant details or highly sensitive annotations should stay tightly controlled unless there’s a clear public health need. For restricted linked records and especially sensitive notes during a rapid intervention or containment action, access should follow minimum necessary access to get the action done rather than blanket access to the whole record. Responders should see only the specific details needed for that task, editing should stay with the assigned case team or a designated lead unless there is an urgent operational reason to widen it, and access should return to the tighter normal level once the immediate action is complete. Each team can edit only the fields or sections they own for their part of the workflow, and anything shared across workflows should be locked or coordinated through the case lead. If a change could affect another team’s work, or it changes a core record like identity, status, exposure linkage, or disposition, it should be routed through the lead rather than edited directly.

slots.value: Timeout should depend on how critical and how common the action is, with routine lookups timing out sooner than larger searches, imports, or cross-record checks. If the user is actively entering data, the system should be more patient in the background, but it still needs to stop waiting at some point and tell them clearly what failed. For outbreak-wide reporting or a large deduplication job, the system should wait longer and use a different failure path, since those can be resumed or rerun without blocking immediate case work. The decision should be based on how often the action is used, how urgently the user needs the result to continue, and whether the work can safely continue in the background. Routine lookups should have short windows because they’re expected to return right away, active data-entry tasks should allow a bit more time so investigators aren’t interrupted in the middle of work, and larger outbreak-wide jobs should have the longest window and be handled more like background processing with status updates instead of making the user wait on the screen.

topics.topic_content: Linking related entities, events, and chains of transmission

slots.value: Connect related entities and events; preserve the core public health workflow so staff can review a signal, assign investigation ownership, document case and contact details, and record actions taken, while centralizing and making more consistent the linking of entities; treat lab reports, case reports, and referrals as related but distinct sources, and allow multiple sources to attach to the same investigation without losing original details. Use a single shared case record with linked entities underneath it so everyone works from the same source of truth; attribute each person's actions, notes, and status changes to their user account and timestamp them; prevent duplicate contacts or exposures by matching on identifiers and let staff merge records when needed; keep conflicting updates in the audit trail and require an authorized reviewer to resolve them before reports are finalized. The shared case should hold the core investigation status and overall summary, while linked people, contacts, exposures, and actions can be edited separately when they belong to different parts of the investigation; editing should be limited to what the investigator's role and assignment allow; linked details such as identifying information, lab results, and sensitive interview notes may need to remain restricted to a smaller group for legal or public health reasons; if a linked record is used in multiple active workflows, edits should be controlled carefully to prevent one team from overwriting information another team still depends on. Anything already committed to the database should not be rolled back just because a later save timed out; preserve unsaved changes, but if the underlying record was already submitted or linked by someone else, conflicting edits should be cleared or flagged for review before resubmitting; sensitive or system-generated fields should be refreshed from the saved record rather than restored from the user's old screen state. Offline records should preserve the original time the action happened, who performed it, and how it relates to the case or contact it belongs to; they should not be re-dated to the time of entry unless that is explicitly noted, and each paper or offline record should carry a unique local identifier or reference so it can be matched back cleanly during reconciliation. Staff can quickly identify who is connected to the event, track the spread and scope, and act on those findings without losing important details; cases, contacts, exposures, and interventions should remain linked together reliably so teams can make timely containment decisions and turn incoming information into coordinated action fast enough to stop further spread.

Locking, approval, and conflict resolution procedure
slots.value: A shared record should be locked or require supervisor approval when a change affects case status, exposure classification, contact tracing assignments, or anything that could change who is notified or what public health action happens next. Approval is also expected when the record is already being edited by someone else, or when the user is trying to change restricted sensitive data. Time-critical containment updates, such as a positive lab result or urgent isolation action, may bypass the restriction if a qualified supervisor or designated responder forces the update, but the system must log exactly why and alert the other users. If a change could affect another team’s work, or it changes a core record like identity, status, exposure linkage, or disposition, it should be routed through the lead rather than edited directly.

slots.key: Action-specific timeout behavior for long-running operations
slots.value: Timeout should vary by action criticality and frequency of use: routine lookups should have short windows because they are expected to return right away, active data-entry tasks should allow a bit more time so investigators are not interrupted in the middle of work, and larger outbreak-wide jobs should have the longest window and be handled more like background processing with status updates instead of making the user wait on the screen. The timeout decision should also consider how urgently the user needs the result to continue and whether the work can safely continue in the background.

slots.value: Bring over enough history to keep active and recently closed investigations usable, including case, contact, exposure, specimen, and intervention records tied to them. For the go-live conversion, full-detail records should cover active cases and recently closed investigations, going back far enough to support continuity and reporting for the current outbreak cycle or a defined retention window. slots.key: Graceful failure and retry behavior for slow operations
slots.value: If a search, save, or common query goes beyond a reasonable threshold, the system should fail gracefully, preserve what the user already entered, and offer a retry instead of making them start over. If it’s still running after the progress indicator has been up for a while, the system should time out based on the kind of action, but not so quickly that it cuts off normal outbreak work. What gets preserved should be whatever the user already typed or selected on that screen, so they don’t lose a partially entered case note, search criteria, or form field values. They should be able to keep working in other parts of the system while the failed action is retried, as long as we haven’t already reserved or locked something that would make that unsafe. Timeout should depend on how critical and how common the action is, with routine lookups timing out sooner than larger searches, imports, or cross-record checks. When the user is actively entering data, the system should be more patient in the background, but it still needs to stop waiting at some point and tell them clearly what failed. Outbreak-wide reporting and large deduplication jobs should wait longer and use a different failure path, since they can be resumed or rerun without blocking immediate case work.

topics.topic_content: Protection of sensitive health information

slots.key: Access control by role and case sensitivity
slots.value: Access should be based on role, jurisdiction, and need to know, with the default being as narrow as possible for anything sensitive or restricted. If a record is tied to a specific investigation, only the assigned team and the people supporting that jurisdiction should be able to view or edit it, and notes with especially sensitive details should be even more limited. Access can be broadened only when it’s necessary for coordinated response or supervision, but things like protected informant details or highly sensitive annotations should stay tightly controlled unless there’s a clear public health need. For restricted linked records and especially sensitive notes during rapid intervention or containment, the practical rule is minimum necessary access to get the action done, not blanket access to the whole record. The intervention team should see only the specific details needed for that task, editing should stay with the assigned case team or a designated lead unless there’s an urgent operational reason to widen it, and access should return to the tighter normal level once the immediate action is complete.

slots.value: When an investigator is offline, the system should let them draft notes and queue certain updates, but anything that could overwrite someone else's work must wait for sync and conflict checking on reconnect. If the case changed while they were away, the system should preserve both the offline submission and the newer online version so a reviewer can reconcile them instead of silently replacing one with the other. Anything authoritative about identity, status, timestamps, linkage, ownership, or audit-related values should be reloaded from the persisted record because those can change while the user is waiting. This includes case status, assigned investigator, last updated time, linked contacts or labs, and any system-set identifiers or flags. Deliberately staged changes that have not been committed yet should not replace the saved value unless the user explicitly confirms them. For offline paper or field-note entries entered later, the event time should stay as the original action time, the later entry time should be recorded separately in the system, and the later entry time should also appear in the audit trail if the delay affects review.

slots.key: Incident readiness milestones and post-incident reconciliation
slots.value: Before an incident starts, the core case, contact, exposure, and reporting workflows should be proven and ready, with access controls and backup procedures in place. During the incident, the expectation shifts to stability, quick updates, and visibility into active work. Immediately after, offline entries should be reconciled, data validated, and a quick status review completed so nothing was missed. Exceptions can apply when a jurisdiction has a hard dependency on a legacy system, a complex data migration, or an integration that must be live from day one, in which case deployment may be sequenced differently or held back until those pieces are ready. Programs with heavier confidentiality or reporting requirements may also need extra validation before go-live, even if that means they do not follow the normal pilot-first order.

slots.key: Critical update exceptions during rapid-response phase
slots.value: Updates may proceed during rapid-response if the interruption is short and controlled and the update prevents a much bigger operational or safety problem, especially when waiting would pose a greater risk than the temporary workflow disruption. Acceptable examples include a security fix or a correction to critical data handling. The staff should know the update is coming, the outage window should be very small, and there should be a clear rollback plan if anything unexpected happens.

In such cases, the change should be the smallest safe change possible and include a rollback plan.

slots.key: Offline access for investigators in low-connectivity settings
slots.value: Offline access should be limited to only the cases and data the investigator already has permission to see, with sensitive fields tightly restricted; investigators can draft notes and queue certain updates while offline, but anything that could overwrite someone else's work must wait for sync and conflict checking when they reconnect; if the case changed while they were away, the system should preserve both the offline submission and the newer online version so a reviewer can reconcile them instead of silently replacing one with the other. During downtime or recovery, staff must be able to capture new cases, contacts, exposures, and critical actions via temporary offline logging or a paper/emergency form, then re-enter those records later without losing timestamps, ownership, or links between records. If the system is recovering, read-only access to existing case details would also be helpful so people can keep working from what’s already known.

slots.key: Graceful failure and retry behavior for slow actions
slots.value: If it is still running after the progress indicator has been up for a while, it should time out based on the kind of action, with the timeout depending on how critical and how common the action is. Routine lookups should time out sooner than larger searches, imports, or cross-record checks. If the user is actively entering data, the system should be more patient in the background, but it still needs to stop waiting at some point and clearly tell them what failed. Outbreak-wide reporting and large deduplication jobs should get a longer wait and a different failure path, since they can be resumed or rerun without blocking immediate case work. The timeout decision should also consider how often the action is used, how urgently the user needs the result to continue, and whether the work can safely continue in the background. Routine lookups should have short windows because they are expected to return right away; active data-entry tasks should allow a bit more time so investigators are not interrupted in the middle of work; larger outbreak-wide jobs should have the longest window and be handled more like background processing, with status updates instead of making the user wait on the screen.
